Missions to comets and asteroids by laun.Giotto: The European probe flew within about 600 km of Halley's Comet in 1986, was hit by dust, and was named for the painter who depicted the comet.
Missions to comets and asteroids by laun.NEAR Shoemaker: It was the first spacecraft to orbit and then, in 2001, land on an asteroid, Eros, though it was never designed to touch down.
Missions to comets and asteroids by laun.Stardust: It flew through the tail of comet Wild 2 and brought dust back to Earth in 2006, captured in a very light material called aerogel.
Missions to comets and asteroids by laun.Hayabusa: Japan's probe returned grains from the asteroid Itokawa in 2010, despite engine failures and a lost lander.
Missions to comets and asteroids by laun.Rosetta: It was the first to orbit a comet, 67P, and put down the lander Philae in 2014, which bounced and ended up in a shadow.
Missions to comets and asteroids by laun.Deep Impact: It fired a copper impactor into comet Tempel 1 on July 4, 2005, letting astronomers see its interior.
Missions to comets and asteroids by laun.Dawn: It was the first spacecraft to orbit two bodies in the asteroid belt, Vesta and the dwarf planet Ceres, using ion engines.
Missions to comets and asteroids by laun.Hayabusa2: It sampled asteroid Ryugu, and its capsule parachuted into the Australian outback in 2020.
Missions to comets and asteroids by laun.OSIRIS-REx: It scooped rubble from the asteroid Bennu and dropped its sample capsule in Utah in 2023.
Missions to comets and asteroids by laun.DART: It rammed the asteroid moon Dimorphos in 2022 and shortened its orbit by about 32 minutes, the first test of planetary defense.

Transplant and artificial-organ firsts.Cornea: The Czech surgeon Eduard Zirm performed the first successful one in 1905, and corneas are usually accepted since they lack blood vessels.
Transplant and artificial-organ firsts.Kidney: The Boston operation was done between identical twins, so the new kidney was not rejected, and surgeon Joseph Murray later won a Nobel.
Transplant and artificial-organ firsts.Lung: The patient in Mississippi lived only 18 days, and it took another two decades for lung transplants to succeed regularly.
Transplant and artificial-organ firsts.Heart: Christiaan Barnard did this in Cape Town, and the patient, Louis Washkansky, lived 18 days after the operation.
Transplant and artificial-organ firsts.Bone marrow: The first successful one treated a child with an immune deficiency, and today it is used for leukemia and other blood cancers.
Transplant and artificial-organ firsts.Heart and lungs together: Stanford surgeons did the first combined operation, which was later used to treat conditions like cystic fibrosis and pulmonary hypertension.
Transplant and artificial-organ firsts.Jarvik-7 artificial heart: Barney Clark, who received it in Utah, lived 112 days, and it showed that artificial hearts could work for a time.
Transplant and artificial-organ firsts.Hand: The first operation was performed in Lyon, France, and the recipient later asked for the hand to be removed.
Transplant and artificial-organ firsts.Face (partial): A French woman, mauled by a dog, received the first partial one in Amiens, with a donor's nose, lips and chin.
Transplant and artificial-organ firsts.Pig heart into a human: A genetically modified pig heart was put into a patient in Maryland, who lived two months and opened the way for animal organs.

Famous poems, by publication year.Paradise Lost: Milton wrote this epic about the fall of Adam and Eve after going completely blind, dictating the verses to helpers. He sold the rights for just £10.
Famous poems, by publication year.Elegy in a Country Churchyard: Thomas Gray's meditation on ordinary rural lives gave the English language the phrase far from the madding crowd's ignoble strife, later borrowed by Hardy.
Famous poems, by publication year.Kubla Khan: Coleridge said he wrote this poem after an opium-influenced dream, then was interrupted by a visitor and forgot the rest, leaving it unfinished.
Famous poems, by publication year.Ozymandias: Shelley's sonnet describes a shattered statue of a forgotten king in the desert, a warning that even the mightiest rulers fade into dust.
Famous poems, by publication year.The Raven: Poe's poem about a talking bird and a grieving scholar made him famous, yet he reportedly earned only about nine dollars for it.
Famous poems, by publication year.Leaves of Grass: Walt Whitman self-published this collection and kept revising it for the rest of his life, producing several editions known as the deathbed edition.
Famous poems, by publication year.Jabberwocky: This Lewis Carroll nonsense poem from Through the Looking-Glass invented words like chortle and galumphing that later entered everyday English.
Famous poems, by publication year.The Road Not Taken: Robert Frost's poem about two paths diverging in a wood is often misread as a celebration of individuality, though he meant it somewhat ironically.
Famous poems, by publication year.The Waste Land: T. S. Eliot's modernist landmark was shaped by Ezra Pound's heavy edits, which cut it to roughly half of its original draft length.
Famous poems, by publication year.Howl: Allen Ginsberg's Beat Generation cry led to an obscenity trial in 1957, which the publisher won, and which helped loosen censorship in America.

Canadian provinces and territories by ar.Prince Edward Island: Prince Edward Island is Canada's smallest province, known as the birthplace of Confederation and for the setting of Anne of Green Gables.
Canadian provinces and territories by ar.New Brunswick: The Bay of Fundy, home of the highest tides in the world, borders this province, and it is Canada's only officially bilingual province.
Canadian provinces and territories by ar.Newfoundland and Labrador: This province includes the island of Newfoundland and mainland Labrador, and its Viking site at L'Anse aux Meadows dates to about 1000 CE.
Canadian provinces and territories by ar.Yukon: This territory is home to the Klondike, where the 1890s gold rush drew tens of thousands of prospectors to Dawson City.
Canadian provinces and territories by ar.Alberta: Alberta is home to the Rocky Mountains and Banff National Park, and it has dinosaur fossils in Dinosaur Provincial Park.
Canadian provinces and territories by ar.British Columbia: This western province has Canada's Pacific coast, including Vancouver and Vancouver Island, and mountain ranges.
Canadian provinces and territories by ar.Ontario: Canada's most populous province contains Toronto, the capital city Ottawa, and the Canadian side of Niagara Falls.
Canadian provinces and territories by ar.Northwest Territories: The Northwest Territories include Great Slave Lake, one of the deepest lakes in North America, and Yellowknife.
Canadian provinces and territories by ar.Quebec: Quebec is the only province with French as its sole official language, and it is Canada's largest province.
Canadian provinces and territories by ar.Nunavut: Created in 1999, Nunavut means our land in Inuktitut, and it is Canada's largest territory, though sparsely populated.

Famous English and British monarchs, by.William the Conqueror: His victory at Hastings changed England; he later ordered the Domesday Book, a survey of landholdings made in 1086.
Famous English and British monarchs, by.Richard the Lionheart: He spent only months of his reign in England, joined the Third Crusade, and was captured on his way home.
Famous English and British monarchs, by.Henry VIII: He had six wives and broke with Rome. His warship Mary Rose sank in 1545 and was raised in 1982.
Famous English and British monarchs, by.Elizabeth I: Her reign saw the defeat of the Spanish Armada in 1588 and a flourishing of theatre, including Shakespeare.
Famous English and British monarchs, by.Charles I: The only English king tried and executed, beheaded in 1649 after losing the Civil War to Parliament.
Famous English and British monarchs, by.Queen Anne: The last Stuart monarch, in whose reign England and Scotland united as Great Britain in 1707.
Famous English and British monarchs, by.George III: He reigned for 59 years and lost the American colonies. Periods of illness later led to a regency.
Famous English and British monarchs, by.Victoria: Her 63-year reign gave the age her name. She was the longest-reigning British monarch until Elizabeth II.
Famous English and British monarchs, by.Elizabeth II: She learned she was queen while in Kenya, and reigned 70 years, the longest of any British monarch.
Famous English and British monarchs, by.Charles III: The oldest person to accede to the British throne, at 73, after a record time as heir apparent.

Surprising latitudes: cities from north.Paris: Paris lies farther north than Montreal, so despite its mild feel it is further from the equator than a city known for brutal winters.
Surprising latitudes: cities from north.Montreal: Montreal sits at about the latitude of Venice and Bordeaux, yet the Atlantic's warm currents give Europe much milder winters.
Surprising latitudes: cities from north.Rome: Rome shares roughly this latitude with Chicago and Boston, though the Mediterranean makes its winters far gentler.
Surprising latitudes: cities from north.Beijing: Beijing is at about the same latitude as Madrid and Philadelphia, but its climate swings far more between summer and winter.
The US capital lies at about the same latitude as Lisbon and Seoul, though it is much colder than Lisbon in winter.
Surprising latitudes: cities from north.Tokyo: Tokyo shares roughly this latitude with Tehran and Las Vegas, three very different climates at the same distance from the equator.
Surprising latitudes: cities from north.Los Angeles: Los Angeles is at about the same latitude as Fez in Morocco and Baghdad, which helps explain its dry, sunny climate.
Surprising latitudes: cities from north.Tel Aviv: Tel Aviv is close to Dallas and Marrakesh in latitude, with a Mediterranean climate that is warm and mild.
Surprising latitudes: cities from north.Cairo: Cairo sits almost level with Houston and Shanghai, but it receives only a few millimeters of rain a year.
Surprising latitudes: cities from north.New Delhi: New Delhi lies north of the Tropic of Cancer, so it is technically outside the tropics, though it is hot enough to feel inside them.

When these mysteries happened.Princes in the Tower vanish: Edward V and his brother vanished from the Tower of London; their uncle Richard III is the chief suspect, though it is still debated.
When these mysteries happened.Roanoke colony found empty: Colonists in what is now North Carolina left only the word CROATOAN carved on a post; what happened to them is still unknown.
When these mysteries happened.Kaspar Hauser appears: A teenager turned up in Nuremberg claiming he had been kept locked in a dark cell; he was stabbed to death in 1833.
When these mysteries happened.Mary Celeste found adrift: Found in the Atlantic with sails set and cargo mostly intact, the ship's lifeboat was gone and no crew was aboard.
When these mysteries happened.Tunguska explosion: Probably a space rock exploding in the air over Siberia, it flattened around 80 million trees across about 2,000 square kilometres.
When these mysteries happened.Flight 19 disappears: Five US Navy torpedo bombers vanished on a training flight, and the incident fed the Bermuda Triangle legend.
When these mysteries happened.Roswell incident: The US military first announced a recovered flying disc, then said weather balloon; it was later linked to Project Mogul.
When these mysteries happened.Dyatlov Pass incident: Nine hikers died in the Urals; a 2021 study suggested a slab avalanche may explain the strange scene.
When these mysteries happened.D. B. Cooper hijacking: A man hijacked a plane, collected $200,000 and parachuted away; he was never identified, though some of the money turned up in 1980.
When these mysteries happened.The Wow! signal: Astronomer Jerry Ehman circled this 72-second radio burst on a printout and wrote 'Wow!'; it has never repeated.

Sugar content of these fruits, by weight.Avocado: Technically a large berry with one seed, it is high in fat rather than sugar.
Sugar content of these fruits, by weight.Lemon: Citric acid gives its sourness, and its juice was used by sailors against scurvy.
Sugar content of these fruits, by weight.Strawberry: Its seeds are on the outside, about 200 per berry, and each is a separate tiny fruit.
Sugar content of these fruits, by weight.Watermelon: It is about 92 percent water, which is why it tastes sweet but low in sugar.
Sugar content of these fruits, by weight.Orange: Oranges are hybrids of pomelo and mandarin, and are not found wild.
Sugar content of these fruits, by weight.Banana: Starch converts to sugar as it ripens, which is why brown ones taste sweeter.
Sugar content of these fruits, by weight.Grapes: Grapes ferment into wine because they carry enough sugar for yeast to work on.
Sugar content of these fruits, by weight.Dried apricots: Drying removes water but not sugar, so it concentrates, and a handful packs a lot.
Sugar content of these fruits, by weight.Raisins: A grape becomes a raisin after sun drying for weeks, which concentrates the sugar.
Sugar content of these fruits, by weight.Medjool dates: Medjool dates were saved from disease in Morocco in 1927 and moved to California.

From tiny to big.Sesame seed: Sesame seeds are tiny, and a single plant produces so many that the phrase Open Sesame in the old tale has been linked to the pods bursting open.
From tiny to big.Grain of rice: A grain of rice is about the length of a thumbnail's width, and rice feeds more than half the world's population.
From tiny to big.Sugar cube: A standard sugar cube is cut to fit tidy serving size, and the first sugar cubes were invented in the 1840s by a Moravian.
From tiny to big.Golf ball: Golf balls have around 300 to 500 dimples, which reduce drag and let the ball fly farther than a smooth ball.
From tiny to big.Soda can (height): A standard 330 ml soda can is surprisingly strong for its thin walls, because its curved dome-shaped bottom resists the pressure of the fizz.
From tiny to big.A4 sheet (long side): A4 comes from the German DIN system, where each size is half the next, and A0 has an area of exactly one square metre.
From tiny to big.Acoustic guitar: A standard acoustic guitar has six strings, and its hollow body works as a resonator that amplifies the strings' sound.
From tiny to big.Front door (height): Most front doors are around 2 metres tall, a standard that has stayed nearly the same for centuries, rooted in human proportions.
From tiny to big.School bus: A full-size school bus in North America is famously painted National School Bus Glossy Yellow, chosen because it's easiest to see at the edge of vision.
From tiny to big.Olympic pool: An Olympic pool is 50 metres long and at least two metres deep, and it holds about 2.5 million litres of water.

Deadliest volcanic eruptions.Eyjafjallajökull 2010: Eyjafjallajökull's ash cloud grounded European flights for days, yet the eruption killed no one directly.
Deadliest volcanic eruptions.Mount St. Helens 1980: Mount St. Helens blew its north face off, and it's the deadliest and most economically destructive volcanic event in US history.
Deadliest volcanic eruptions.Pinatubo 1991: Pinatubo erupted just after Typhoon Yunya hit, and an early warning saved many thousands of lives.
Deadliest volcanic eruptions.Kelud, Java 1919: Kelud has erupted many times, and its crater lake produces deadly mudflows called lahars, so tunnels were built to drain it.
Deadliest volcanic eruptions.Laki, Iceland 1783: Laki's gas cloud poisoned grass, and the resulting famine killed a quarter of Iceland's population.
Deadliest volcanic eruptions.Unzen, Japan 1792: Mount Unzen's lava dome collapse caused a tsunami in Japan, in what is called the Shimabara catastrophe.
Deadliest volcanic eruptions.Nevado del Ruiz 1985: Nevado del Ruiz's eruption melted glacier ice, and mudflows buried the town of Armero, killing most of its residents.
Deadliest volcanic eruptions.Mount Pelée 1902: Mount Pelée destroyed the town of Saint-Pierre in Martinique in minutes, and only a handful of people survived.
Deadliest volcanic eruptions.Krakatoa 1883: Krakatoa's explosion was heard nearly 5,000 km away, and tsunamis killed most of the victims.
Deadliest volcanic eruptions.Tambora 1815: Tambora's 1815 eruption killed tens of thousands directly and many more from famine, and it triggered a global cooling.

Caribbean countries by area.Saint Kitts and Nevis: The smallest country in the Americas by area and population, it is home to Brimstone Hill Fortress, a UNESCO World Heritage Site above the sea.
Caribbean countries by area.Barbados: Barbados is among the places credited with early commercial rum production, and it is also the birthplace of pop star Rihanna, who it declared a national hero.
Caribbean countries by area.Saint Lucia: Often said to be the only sovereign state named after a woman, it has twin volcanic Pitons and produced two Nobel laureates, Arthur Lewis and Derek Walcott.
Caribbean countries by area.Dominica: Known as the Nature Isle, it has a hot Boiling Lake, and its flag features the Sisserou parrot, making it one of the few flags with purple.
Caribbean countries by area.Trinidad and Tobago: Trinidad is the birthplace of the steelpan, the only acoustic instrument invented in the 20th century, which was first hammered out of oil drums.
Caribbean countries by area.Jamaica: Jamaica gave the world reggae, Usain Bolt, and Blue Mountain coffee, grown high in the mist above Kingston.
Caribbean countries by area.Bahamas: Spread across about 700 islands, it is where Columbus's 1492 landfall most likely happened, and its shallow, clear water is famously turquoise.
Caribbean countries by area.Haiti: In 1804 this country declared independence after the only successful slave revolt to found a nation, becoming the first Black-led republic.
Caribbean countries by area.Dominican Republic: Santo Domingo here is the oldest permanent European settlement in the Americas, and its Colonial Zone houses the hemisphere's oldest cathedral.
Caribbean countries by area.Cuba: Cuba is the largest Caribbean island, and the world's smallest bird, the bee hummingbird, which weighs about as much as a dime, lives only here.

Alkanes by number of carbon atoms.Methane: It is the main part of natural gas, and cow burps release plenty of it, making it a potent greenhouse gas.
Alkanes by number of carbon atoms.Ethane: The second-largest part of natural gas, it is mainly used to make ethylene, the building block of many plastics.
Alkanes by number of carbon atoms.Propane: It turns to liquid under modest pressure, which is why camping cylinders can store so much of it.
Alkanes by number of carbon atoms.Butane: The name comes from butyric acid, first found in rancid butter; it fuels many lighters.
Alkanes by number of carbon atoms.Pentane: A liquid at room temperature, it boils at about 36 °C, so it evaporates quickly.
Alkanes by number of carbon atoms.Hexane: It is used to extract cooking oil from soybeans and other seeds.
Alkanes by number of carbon atoms.Heptane: It defines zero on the octane rating scale, because it knocks terribly in engines.
Alkanes by number of carbon atoms.Octane: Its branched form, iso-octane, defines 100 on the octane scale, which is what pump numbers refer to.
Alkanes by number of carbon atoms.Nonane: Nonane has 35 structural isomers, and the count explodes as more carbons are added.
Alkanes by number of carbon atoms.Decane: Diesel is a mix of longer chains, and this molecule sits at the light end of that range.

Earliest evidence of these foods and dri.Bread: Flatbread remains from Jordan's Shubayqa 1 show hunter-gatherers made bread before farming.
Earliest evidence of these foods and dri.Beer: Residues at Göbekli Tepe suggest brewing may predate farming; some think it drove grain cultivation.
Earliest evidence of these foods and dri.Wine: Residue from jars in Georgia shows that wine was made in the Caucasus some 8,000 years ago, among the oldest on record.
Earliest evidence of these foods and dri.Cheese: Fatty residue on pottery sieves in Poland shows early farmers made cheese, which contains less lactose than milk.
Earliest evidence of these foods and dri.Popcorn: Ancient popped kernels from the coast of Peru are about this old, and older ones come from Mexican caves.
Earliest evidence of these foods and dri.Cacao drink: Residue on Ecuadorian pottery from the Mayo-Chinchipe culture suggests chocolate began in the Amazon.
Earliest evidence of these foods and dri.Noodles: A 4,000-year-old bowl of millet noodles was found at Lajia, China, still holding the long, thin strands.
Earliest evidence of these foods and dri.Coffee drinking: Sufi monasteries in Yemen drank coffee to stay awake during night-time prayers, and the habit then spread through the Middle East.
Earliest evidence of these foods and dri.Canned food: Cans were opened with hammer and chisel for decades; Nicolas Appert's canning method came first.
Earliest evidence of these foods and dri.Solid chocolate bar: J. S. Fry & Sons of Bristol made the first mass-produced eating chocolate bar.

Medicine cabinet brands, by launch year.Listerine: Named after Joseph Lister, the antiseptic pioneer, it was first sold as a surgical antiseptic and even marketed as a floor cleaner.
Medicine cabinet brands, by launch year.Aspirin (Bayer): The name combines "acetyl" with Spiraea, a plant source of salicin, the painkiller's natural relative.
Medicine cabinet brands, by launch year.Alka-Seltzer: Made by Miles Laboratories in Elkhart, Indiana. Its Plop plop fizz fizz jingle is one of advertising's best known.
Medicine cabinet brands, by launch year.Tylenol: The name comes from the chemical's full name, N-acetyl-para-aminophenol, also called acetaminophen or paracetamol.
Medicine cabinet brands, by launch year.NyQuil: Made by Vicks, the company that began with a North Carolina pharmacist's VapoRub.
Medicine cabinet brands, by launch year.Advil: It brought ibuprofen, which was discovered by the British company Boots, to American shelves without a prescription.
Medicine cabinet brands, by launch year.Claritin (US): Loratadine, a non-drowsy antihistamine, went over the counter in the US in 2002.
Medicine cabinet brands, by launch year.Viagra: It was tested at Pfizer as a heart drug for angina, and its best-known side effect was noticed during trials.
Medicine cabinet brands, by launch year.Botox (cosmetic use): Botulinum toxin was first used to treat eye muscle disorders. Cosmetic use was approved in 2002.
Medicine cabinet brands, by launch year.Ozempic: Semaglutide mimics the gut hormone GLP-1. It was meant for type 2 diabetes but became hugely popular for weight loss.

When these symbols and punctuation marks.Ampersand (&): It began as a ligature of the Latin 'et'; schoolchildren once recited it as the alphabet's 27th letter.
When these symbols and punctuation marks.Question mark: One theory holds it came from monks abbreviating the Latin word 'quaestio', stacking a q over an o.
When these symbols and punctuation marks.Exclamation mark: Printers called it the 'note of admiration', and typewriters lacked a key, so typists combined a period and apostrophe.
When these symbols and punctuation marks.Semicolon: Venetian printer Aldus Manutius introduced it, in a book of Pietro Bembo's, to mark a pause longer than a comma.
When these symbols and punctuation marks.Equals sign: Robert Recorde chose two parallel lines because, he wrote, no two things could be more equal.
When these symbols and punctuation marks.Dollar sign: Its origin is debated; a popular theory ties it to the Spanish peso, whose abbreviation was written as 'ps'.
When these symbols and punctuation marks.Interrobang (‽): Martin K. Speckter coined the name for this combined question and exclamation mark, and few fonts include it.
When these symbols and punctuation marks.@ in email addresses: Ray Tomlinson picked it to separate the user's name from the computer's name in networked email.
When these symbols and punctuation marks.Euro sign (€): Its design echoes the Greek epsilon crossed by two lines, and notes and coins arrived in 2002.
When these symbols and punctuation marks.Hashtag on Twitter: Chris Messina suggested grouping tweets with a pound sign, and Twitter later made the hashtag a clickable link.

Number of stars on each flag.Vietnam: The single yellow star on red is said to stand for the five groups of workers: peasants, workers, soldiers, intellectuals and youth.
Number of stars on each flag.Philippines: The three stars stand for Luzon, the Visayas and Mindanao, and flying the flag upside down signals war.
Number of stars on each flag.New Zealand: Four red stars form the Southern Cross, and a 2016 referendum kept the flag.
Number of stars on each flag.China: The big star stands for the Communist Party and the four small ones for social classes, in a design by Zeng Liansong.
Number of stars on each flag.Australia: Five stars form the Southern Cross, and a seven-pointed Commonwealth Star makes six.
Number of stars on each flag.Venezuela: A star was added in 2006 for Guayana province, a nod to Bolívar's plan.
Number of stars on each flag.Cape Verde: The ten stars in a circle stand for the main islands, and the blue stands for the ocean.
Number of stars on each flag.European Union: The number is fixed at twelve whatever the membership, as a symbol of perfection and unity.
Number of stars on each flag.Brazil: The stars stand for the states and the federal district, arranged as the sky over Rio on 15 November 1889.
Number of stars on each flag.United States: A 17-year-old Ohio student, Robert Heft, designed the 50-star flag for a school project.

Legendary diamonds by weight.Hope Diamond: This deep blue stone is cursed in legend. It was cut from the French Blue, stolen in 1792, and since 1958 it has been on show at the Smithsonian.
Legendary diamonds by weight.Sancy: Its earliest history is legend, said to have belonged to Charles the Bold of Burgundy. This pale yellow gem later passed through English and French royal hands and is now at the Louvre.
Legendary diamonds by weight.Koh-i-Noor: Its name is Persian for "Mountain of Light". It is part of the British Crown Jewels, set in the Queen Mother's crown, and is claimed by several nations.
Legendary diamonds by weight.Regent: Found in India around 1698, it later adorned Napoleon's sword hilt. It is one of the most famous stones of the French crown jewels, now in the Louvre.
Legendary diamonds by weight.Orlov: Part of the Russian imperial scepter, this stone is named for Count Orlov, and is said to have been an eye of a Hindu idol.
Legendary diamonds by weight.Great Star of Africa: This gem is also named Cullinan I. It's the largest polished diamond from the Cullinan, and part of the British Sceptre with Cross.
Legendary diamonds by weight.Golden Jubilee: The largest faceted diamond in the world. It's a brownish gem owned by the Thai royal family, and was once named the Unnamed Brown.
Legendary diamonds by weight.Excelsior (rough): Found at South Africa's Jagersfontein mine in 1893, it was the largest diamond ever discovered until the Cullinan turned up in 1905.
Legendary diamonds by weight.Lesedi La Rona (rough): A recent discovery from Botswana in 2015, in the Karowe mine. The 1,109-carat rough, the biggest found in over a century, was sold in 2017.
Legendary diamonds by weight.Cullinan (rough): Found in South Africa in 1905, it's the largest gem-quality rough diamond ever found. It was cut into nine major stones and about 100 smaller ones.

ASCII codes of these characters.Space: The first printable character, code 32, is the blank. It is invisible, yet it separates every word you read, and many programmers call it whitespace.
ASCII codes of these characters.# (hash): Also called the pound sign, number sign or octothorpe. It marks hashtags and comments in many programming languages, and on phone keypads it's the "pound key".
ASCII codes of these characters.& (ampersand): The ampersand, from the Latin "et", meaning "and". It was once the 27th letter of the English alphabet, ending the alphabet recitation.
ASCII codes of these characters.Digit zero: The code for the digit zero is 48, so digits 0 to 9 run from 48 to 57, and programmers subtract 48 to turn a digit character into its number.
ASCII codes of these characters.@ (at sign): The at sign was rare until Ray Tomlinson picked it for email addresses in 1971. In Italian it is called "chiocciola", meaning snail.
ASCII codes of these characters.Capital A: Capitals run from 65 to 90. In ASCII, a capital differs from its lowercase form by exactly 32, a single bit, which makes case conversion simple.
ASCII codes of these characters.Capital Z: The last capital letter is 90, and the capital letters occupy 26 consecutive spots, and lowercase letters begin 32 places further on.
ASCII codes of these characters.Lowercase a: Lowercase letters begin at 97, exactly 32 more than the capitals, so flipping one bit of the code changes a letter's case.
ASCII codes of these characters.Lowercase z: The last lowercase letter is 122, and after it come four punctuation characters: curly braces, a vertical bar, and the tilde.
ASCII codes of these characters.~ (tilde): The tilde is the last printable character. After it, code 127, comes DEL, a control character originally used to erase paper tape.

Silly units of length.Beard-second: A beard-second is how far a beard grows in a second, about the width of a few atoms, and it's a classic joke unit.
Silly units of length.Mickey (mouse movement): The mouse-movement unit is about the width of a human hair, and was named after the Mickey Mouse mouse of early computing.
Silly units of length.Grace Hopper's nanosecond: Admiral Grace Hopper handed out lengths of wire to show how far light travels in a billionth of a second.
Silly units of length.Smoot: Named for MIT student Oliver Smoot, who was laid end to end across the Harvard Bridge in 1958 to measure it.
Silly units of length.American football field: A gridiron football field is 100 yards between the goal lines, and 120 yards including the end zones.
Silly units of length.Sheppey: A joke unit said to be the farthest distance at which a sheep is still recognizable as a sheep.
Silly units of length.Marathon: The marathon is 42.195 km because the 1908 London Olympic course ran from Windsor Castle to the royal box at the stadium.
Silly units of length.Light-second: Light travels this far each second, which is about three-quarters of the way to the Moon.
Silly units of length.Astronomical unit: Defined from the average Earth-Sun distance, and light takes about eight minutes to cross it.
Silly units of length.Light-year: The distance light travels in a year, and the nearest star beyond the Sun is about four and a bit of these away.

When these famous battles were fought.Kadesh: Ramesses II fought the Hittites here, and the later treaty is the oldest surviving peace treaty known, with copies in both languages.
When these famous battles were fought.Marathon: A smaller Athenian army beat a Persian force here, and the run to announce the victory inspired the marathon legend.
When these famous battles were fought.Gaugamela: Alexander the Great routed Darius III on open ground, ending the Persian Empire's hold on the Near East.
When these famous battles were fought.Cannae: Hannibal's double envelopment crushed a larger Roman army, and it is still studied in military schools.
When these famous battles were fought.Actium: Octavian's fleet defeated Antony and Cleopatra here, which set the stage for the Roman Empire.
When these famous battles were fought.Teutoburg Forest: Germanic tribes ambushed three Roman legions in forest and bog, and Augustus reportedly cried out for his lost legions.
When these famous battles were fought.Adrianople: Gothic cavalry crushed the Eastern Roman army and killed Emperor Valens, a key blow to the empire.
When these famous battles were fought.Tours: Charles Martel stopped a Muslim army advancing from Iberia in France, and he is celebrated as a savior of Europe.
When these famous battles were fought.Hastings: William of Normandy defeated King Harold, who was reportedly hit by an arrow, and the battle is shown in the Bayeux Tapestry.
When these famous battles were fought.Agincourt: Henry V's English archers beat a much larger French army in the mud, and Shakespeare made it famous.

When these popes took office.Leo the Great: Leo I persuaded Attila the Hun to turn back from Italy in 452, and he is one of two popes called the Great.
When these popes took office.Gregory the Great: Gregory the Great sent missionaries to England, and Gregorian chant is named after him, though he probably didn't write it.
When these popes took office.Leo III: Leo III crowned Charlemagne emperor on Christmas Day in the year 800, reviving a western empire.
When these popes took office.Sylvester II: Sylvester II was a scholar who brought Arabic numerals and the abacus to wider notice in Europe, and he was known as Gerbert of Aurillac.
When these popes took office.Gregory VII: Gregory VII clashed with Emperor Henry IV, who stood barefoot in the snow at Canossa to seek forgiveness.
When these popes took office.Innocent III: Innocent III was perhaps the most powerful pope of the Middle Ages, and he launched the Fourth Crusade and approved the Franciscans.
When these popes took office.Boniface VIII: Boniface VIII feuded with the king of France, and Dante placed him in Hell in the Divine Comedy.
When these popes took office.Martin V: Martin V was elected at the Council of Constance, which ended the Western Schism with its rival popes.
When these popes took office.Sixtus IV: Sixtus IV built the Sistine Chapel, which is named for him, and he approved the Spanish Inquisition.
When these popes took office.Alexander VI (Borgia): The Borgia pope took office the same year Columbus reached the Americas, and his family became a byword for scandal.

When these instrument makers were founde.Zildjian: A family of Istanbul cymbal makers founded it, and they have kept their secret metal alloy within the family for centuries.
When these instrument makers were founde.C. F. Martin: This German immigrant's Pennsylvania firm still makes acoustic guitars, and helped invent the big dreadnought body.
When these instrument makers were founde.Steinway and Sons: Heinrich Steinweg anglicised his name after moving to New York, and his pianos became the concert-hall standard.
When these instrument makers were founde.Yamaha: It began as a reed organ maker in Hamamatsu, Japan, and later expanded into pianos, motorcycles and electronics.
When these instrument makers were founde.Gibson: Its Les Paul guitar was named after the guitarist and inventor who helped design it in the early 1950s.
When these instrument makers were founde.Ludwig drums: Ringo Starr's Ludwig kit, with the band's name on the bass drum, appeared on the Beatles' Ed Sullivan Show debut.
When these instrument makers were founde.Rickenbacker: The firm built the 'Frying Pan', one of the first commercially made electric guitars, a cast aluminium design.
When these instrument makers were founde.Fender: Leo Fender began as a radio repairman, and ironically could not play guitar himself, even as his Telecaster became a classic.
When these instrument makers were founde.Marshall amps: Drum shop owner Jim Marshall made the first amps to match what London guitarists, such as Pete Townshend, wanted.
When these instrument makers were founde.Roland: Founder Ikutaro Kakehashi's company made the TR-808 drum machine, a flop at first that later shaped hip-hop and dance music.

When these Roman structures were built.Cloaca Maxima sewer: Rome's great drain, said to have been built by the Etruscan kings, was so well built that part of it still carries water today.
When these Roman structures were built.Via Appia: Rome's oldest major road was called the 'queen of roads', and it ran roughly 560 km, linking Rome to Brindisi on the coast.
When these Roman structures were built.Theatre of Pompey: This was Rome's first permanent stone theatre, and Julius Caesar was assassinated in a room attached to it.
When these Roman structures were built.Ara Pacis: Emperor Augustus built this altar of peace to celebrate his victories, and its carved reliefs include portraits of his own family.
When these Roman structures were built.Colosseum: Originally named the Flavian Amphitheatre, it could hold perhaps 50,000 spectators, and its retractable awnings were operated by sailors.
When these Roman structures were built.Trajan's Column: Its spiral frieze shows Rome's victory in Dacia, and it is nearly 30 metres tall; the emperor's ashes were placed beneath it.
When these Roman structures were built.Hadrian's Mausoleum: Later converted into a papal fortress, it became Castel Sant'Angelo, named after the angel said to have appeared above it in a plague.
When these Roman structures were built.Baths of Caracalla: These huge public baths could hold well over a thousand bathers, and they included libraries, gardens and exercise courts.
When these Roman structures were built.Aurelian Walls: The city wall, ordered when invaders threatened, is about 19 km long and still stands, much of it in remarkably good condition.
When these Roman structures were built.Arch of Constantine: This triumphal arch honours Constantine's victory at the Milvian Bridge, and it reused decorations pulled from earlier monuments.

Months of the Islamic calendar.Muharram: One of four sacred months when fighting is forbidden; its tenth day, Ashura, is significant to both Sunni and Shia Muslims.
Months of the Islamic calendar.Safar: Often explained as 'empty' or 'yellow'; Islamic teaching rejects the old superstition that it brings bad luck.
Months of the Islamic calendar.Rabi al-Awwal: Many Muslims mark Mawlid, the Prophet Muhammad's birthday, on the 12th of this month, whose name means 'first spring'.
Months of the Islamic calendar.Jumada al-Ula: Its name is linked to a word for 'frozen' or 'dry', perhaps from when the months were named in a cold season.
Months of the Islamic calendar.Rajab: Another sacred month; many Muslims remember Isra and Mi'raj, the Prophet's night journey, on its 27th night.
Months of the Islamic calendar.Sha'ban: The month before Ramadan, when many Muslims begin to fast and pray more as preparation.
Months of the Islamic calendar.Ramadan: Because the lunar year is about 11 days shorter than the solar one, this month of fasting drifts through the seasons.
Months of the Islamic calendar.Shawwal: It opens with Eid al-Fitr, the festival ending the fast, and many Muslims fast six extra days in it.
Months of the Islamic calendar.Dhu al-Qa'dah: A sacred month whose name means roughly 'the one of rest'; Arabs traditionally stopped fighting before the pilgrimage.
Months of the Islamic calendar.Dhu al-Hijjah: The month of Hajj, the pilgrimage to Mecca, and it ends the year with Eid al-Adha.

Dartboard numbers, clockwise from the to.1: Next to 20, it is a poor miss, and the board's layout punishes inaccurate throwing.
Dartboard numbers, clockwise from the to.2: A leg must end on a double or the bullseye, so this number is a common finishing target.
Dartboard numbers, clockwise from the to.4: A perfect round of three treble 20s scores 180, the highest possible three-dart score.
Dartboard numbers, clockwise from the to.6: The bullseye is hung 1.73 m (5 ft 8 in) from the floor, to its center.
Dartboard numbers, clockwise from the to.10: The throwing line, called the oche, is 2.37 m from the board, and the word's origin is uncertain.
Dartboard numbers, clockwise from the to.13: A perfect leg of 501 takes only nine darts, which is rare even among professionals.
Dartboard numbers, clockwise from the to.15: The bull's outer ring counts 25 and the inner bull 50, which counts as a double.
Dartboard numbers, clockwise from the to.17: Players often use 17 or 19 as secondary targets in the game Cricket, which uses 15 to 20 and the bull.
Dartboard numbers, clockwise from the to.18: Placed beside 4 and 1, the layout alternates high and low so near-misses cost points.
Dartboard numbers, clockwise from the to.20: Folk history credits carpenter Brian Gamlin with the 1896 layout, which puts 20 between small 1 and 5 to punish wild throws.

How many do you have? Small numbers.Kidneys: You can live a healthy life with just one, which is why living kidney donors are possible and common.
How many do you have? Small numbers.Semicircular canals per ear: Fluid in these three looping tubes senses head rotation, which is why spinning around leaves you dizzy.
How many do you have? Small numbers.Lobes in both lungs: The right lung has three lobes and the left only two, leaving room for the heart on that side.
How many do you have? Small numbers.Neck vertebrae: Nearly all mammals have seven, whether giraffes, whales or mice; only manatees and a few sloths differ.
How many do you have? Small numbers.Fingers: Having ten of them is probably why humans came to count in base ten, a habit found across cultures.
How many do you have? Small numbers.Pairs of ribs: Twelve pairs, with the lowest two 'floating ribs' not attached to the breastbone at the front.
How many do you have? Small numbers.Baby teeth: They are already forming in the jaw before birth, and usually appear around six months of age.
How many do you have? Small numbers.Pairs of chromosomes: Humans have 23 pairs, while a dog has 39, so chromosome count says nothing about complexity.
How many do you have? Small numbers.Pairs of spinal nerves: Each pair serves a strip of skin called a dermatome, which doctors map to pinpoint nerve damage.
How many do you have? Small numbers.Adult teeth: Thirty-two includes four wisdom teeth, which many people never develop or have removed.

Average yearly rainfall: drizzle to delu.Arica, Chile: Arica sits in the Atacama region, one of the driest places on Earth, where some years pass with essentially no measurable rain at all.
Average yearly rainfall: drizzle to delu.Cairo: Cairo gets so little rain that its buildings and streets are barely designed for it; a few showers can cause flooding and traffic chaos.
Average yearly rainfall: drizzle to delu.Las Vegas: Las Vegas is in the Mojave Desert, yet flash floods are a real threat because dry, hard ground sheds water instead of absorbing it.
Average yearly rainfall: drizzle to delu.Los Angeles: Los Angeles gets most of its rain in winter, and the concrete channel of the Los Angeles River was built to speed floodwater to the sea.
Average yearly rainfall: drizzle to delu.London: London's reputation for rain is exaggerated: it gets less annual rainfall than Rome, Sydney or New York City.
Average yearly rainfall: drizzle to delu.Seattle: Seattle is known for gray drizzle, but it has far fewer inches of rain than the Southeast US; it just rains on many days.
Average yearly rainfall: drizzle to delu.Tokyo: Tokyo's rainy season, called tsuyu, arrives around June, bringing weeks of humid, grey weather that nurtures the rice crop.
Average yearly rainfall: drizzle to delu.Singapore: Singapore sits almost on the equator and gets rain in every month, with frequent short, heavy afternoon thunderstorms.
Average yearly rainfall: drizzle to delu.Hilo, Hawaii: Hilo is among the wettest US cities, as trade winds push moist air up Mauna Kea and Mauna Loa and drop rain on the windward side.
Average yearly rainfall: drizzle to delu.Mawsynram, India: Mawsynram in Meghalaya is often called the wettest place on Earth; locals wear woven bamboo-and-leaf shields to stay dry in the monsoon.

More elements by atomic number.Lithium: The lightest metal floats on water, powers rechargeable batteries and is used in medication for mood disorders.
More elements by atomic number.Fluorine: The most reactive element of all was isolated in 1886 by Henri Moissan, who won a Nobel Prize for it.
More elements by atomic number.Phosphorus: Hennig Brand discovered it in 1669 by boiling down urine, and he saw it glow in the dark.
More elements by atomic number.Calcium: The name comes from calx, Latin for lime, and the metal makes up much of your bones and teeth.
More elements by atomic number.Zinc: Mixed with copper it makes brass, and a coating of it protects steel from rust in galvanising.
More elements by atomic number.Bromine: With mercury, it is one of only two elements that are liquid at room temperature, and its name means 'stench'.
More elements by atomic number.Tin: Its symbol, Sn, comes from the Latin stannum, and bronze made with it gave the Bronze Age its name.
More elements by atomic number.Iodine: Its vapour is purple, and the name comes from the Greek for violet.
More elements by atomic number.Platinum: Spanish conquistadors called it 'platina', or little silver, because they saw it as a nuisance in gold mining.
More elements by atomic number.Plutonium: Named for Pluto, it fuelled the Nagasaki bomb, and was discovered in 1940, a decade after Pluto itself.

When these wars broke out.Thirty Years' War: It began as a Bohemian religious conflict and devastated Central Europe; parts of Germany lost up to a third of their people.
When these wars broke out.English Civil War: Parliament fought King Charles I, who was executed in 1649, leaving England briefly without a monarch.
When these wars broke out.Seven Years' War: Often called the first world war since it was fought across Europe, the Americas, Africa and India.
When these wars broke out.Crimean War: Florence Nightingale rose to fame nursing wounded soldiers, and Tennyson wrote of the Charge of the Light Brigade.
When these wars broke out.American Civil War: The deadliest US war, with roughly 620,000 soldiers dead, which ended slavery after four years.
When these wars broke out.Franco-Prussian War: It ended in a Prussian win and the proclamation of the German Empire in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles.
When these wars broke out.Second Boer War: Britain used concentration camps against Boer civilians, where tens of thousands died of disease.
When these wars broke out.Russo-Japanese War: Japan's victory stunned the world as the first modern Asian power to beat a European great power, sealed at the sea battle of Tsushima.
When these wars broke out.Spanish Civil War: Picasso's Guernica responded to the bombing of a Basque town; the war ended in 1939 with Franco's dictatorship.
When these wars broke out.Korean War: It ended with only an armistice in 1953, never a peace treaty, so the two Koreas are technically still at war.

When these gums and mints came out.Altoids: Said to date to 1780s England and marketed as curiously strong mints in a distinctive tin.
When these gums and mints came out.Wrigley's Spearmint: William Wrigley Jr. started by giving gum away as a bonus with his baking powder.
When these gums and mints came out.Dubble Bubble: Walter Diemer invented it, and made it pink because that was the only dye he had on hand.
When these gums and mints came out.Bazooka: Wrapped with a Bazooka Joe comic, it was named for the comedian Bob Burns's musical instrument.
When these gums and mints came out.Trident: One of the first sugarless gums, it was marketed for dental health with the four out of five dentists slogan.
When these gums and mints came out.Tic Tac: Italian maker Ferrero named them for the sound they make when shaken; each has about 2 calories.
When these gums and mints came out.Bubble Yum: The first soft bubble gum, introduced by Life Savers, and a popular urban myth about spider eggs nearly sank it.
When these gums and mints came out.Hubba Bubba: Wrigley's bubble gum promised, big bubble, no trouble.
When these gums and mints came out.Extra: Wrigley's sugar-free brand, and chewing sugar-free gum after meals can boost saliva, which helps neutralize mouth acid.
When these gums and mints came out.Ice Breakers: The Hershey brand known for a Duo mint, with mint outside and a gum center.

From breeze to monster storm, by wind sp.Fresh breeze: Force 5 on the Beaufort scale, devised by Admiral Francis Beaufort in 1805, where small trees begin to sway.
From breeze to monster storm, by wind sp.Tropical depression: Storms at this stage get a number, not a name, until winds reach 63 km/h.
From breeze to monster storm, by wind sp.Tropical storm: At this strength a storm gets a name from a rotating list kept by the World Meteorological Organization.
From breeze to monster storm, by wind sp.Category 1 hurricane: The Saffir-Simpson scale is named for an engineer, Herbert Saffir, and a meteorologist, Robert Simpson.
From breeze to monster storm, by wind sp.Category 2 hurricane: Storm surge, rather than wind, is often the deadliest part of a hurricane at this level and above.
From breeze to monster storm, by wind sp.Category 3 hurricane: The first rung counted as a 'major' hurricane, a category Katrina was at landfall in 2005.
From breeze to monster storm, by wind sp.Category 4 hurricane: Hurricane Harvey made landfall in Texas at this strength in 2017, then stalled and flooded Houston.
From breeze to monster storm, by wind sp.Category 5 hurricane: The scale has no category 6, since there's no official ceiling, and the top rung already means catastrophic damage.
From breeze to monster storm, by wind sp.Hurricane Patricia at peak: This 2015 eastern Pacific storm was the strongest hurricane ever measured in the Western Hemisphere, yet it caused less damage than feared.
From breeze to monster storm, by wind sp.Record gust, Barrow Island: Tropical Cyclone Olivia in 1996 produced this gust, which stood as the highest recorded surface wind speed for decades.

Spacecraft firsts.First artificial satellite: Sputnik 1 was a polished metal sphere that beeped as it orbited, and it started the space race.
Spacecraft firsts.First weather satellite: TIROS-1 sent back the first TV pictures of Earth's clouds from space, and it changed how we forecast the weather.
Spacecraft firsts.First live transatlantic TV: Telstar 1 relayed the first live TV across the Atlantic, and it was also the focus of a popular instrumental song.
Spacecraft firsts.First geostationary satellite: Syncom 3 was the first geostationary satellite, and it hovered above one spot, and it broadcast the Tokyo Olympics.
Spacecraft firsts.First GPS satellite: The first GPS satellite, Navstar 1, launched in 1978, and it took until 1995 for the whole system to be fully operational.
Spacecraft firsts.First landing on an asteroid: NEAR Shoemaker touched down on the asteroid Eros, though it wasn't designed for landing, and it kept working afterward.
Spacecraft firsts.Voyager 1 enters interstellar: Voyager 1 crossed into interstellar space, and it's the most distant human-made object, still sending data.
Spacecraft firsts.First landing on a comet: Rosetta's lander Philae touched down on Comet 67P, and it bounced twice before landing in a shadowy spot.
Spacecraft firsts.First orbital booster landing: SpaceX's Falcon 9 landed upright after launch, and it made rockets reusable, which lowered costs.
Spacecraft firsts.First private Moon landing: Intuitive Machines' Odysseus lander touched down near the Moon's south pole, and it landed on its side.

Length of one round, quarter or half.Pro boxing round: Three-minute rounds with one-minute breaks come from the Queensberry Rules of 1867, which shaped modern boxing.
Length of one round, quarter or half.UFC round: Title fights run five rounds of five minutes, while non-title bouts have three. The cage is an octagon.
Length of one round, quarter or half.Rugby sevens half: The sevens halves are short, so a match is only 14 minutes, though finals are played in 10-minute halves.
Length of one round, quarter or half.Water polo quarter: Four 8-minute quarters, but the clock stops on whistles, so real time is far longer. Players tread water and never touch the bottom.
Length of one round, quarter or half.NBA quarter: Twelve-minute quarters. The league adopted a 24-second shot clock in 1954 to stop teams stalling with a lead.
Length of one round, quarter or half.NFL quarter: Fifteen-minute quarters, but the clock stops constantly. A Wall Street Journal study found about 11 minutes of actual play per game.
Length of one round, quarter or half.NHL period: Twenty-minute periods. Regular-season overtime is a short five minutes of 3-on-3 play.
Length of one round, quarter or half.Gaelic football half: Senior inter-county matches have two 35-minute halves. The All-Ireland final at Croke Park draws over 80,000 fans.
Length of one round, quarter or half.Rugby union half: Two halves of 40 minutes, but play continues after time until the ball goes dead, so the final whistle never comes mid-move.
Length of one round, quarter or half.Soccer half: Referees add stoppage time. At Qatar 2022 matches regularly ran ten or more minutes past 90, a recent break from habit.

How long these empires lasted.Alexander's empire: Spanning Greece to India, it broke into Hellenistic kingdoms when Alexander died in Babylon at 32.
How long these empires lasted.Sui dynasty of China: It built the Grand Canal, then collapsed from costly wars, clearing the way for the Tang.
How long these empires lasted.Aztec Empire: Founded Tenochtitlan in 1325, the Triple Alliance formed in 1428, and Cortés ended it in 1521.
How long these empires lasted.Achaemenid Persia: Founded by Cyrus the Great, it built the Royal Road and fell to Alexander in 330 BC.
How long these empires lasted.Song dynasty of China: Invented movable-type printing and paper money, and used gunpowder weapons in war.
How long these empires lasted.Han dynasty of China: It gave the Chinese majority its name, the Han, and opened the Silk Road to the West.
How long these empires lasted.Western Roman Empire: Fell in 476 when Odoacer deposed the boy emperor Romulus Augustulus.
How long these empires lasted.Ottoman Empire: It conquered Constantinople in 1453 and lasted until 1922, when the Turkish Republic replaced it.
How long these empires lasted.Byzantine Empire: It never called itself Byzantine; its citizens called themselves Romans.
How long these empires lasted.Pharaonic Egypt: Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid.

When these food guides, prizes and shows.The Michelin Guide: Created by the tyre company in 1900 to encourage motorists to drive, it was originally given away free. It listed mechanics and petrol stops.
When these food guides, prizes and shows.Michelin stars: Michelin began rating restaurants with a single star in 1926. Three stars means exceptional cuisine worth a special journey.
When these food guides, prizes and shows.Gourmet magazine: This American food magazine ran for almost seven decades before it was abruptly shut in 2009. It was a favourite of foodies.
When these food guides, prizes and shows.Zagat guide: A couple began it by collecting restaurant ratings from friends in New York City. Its burgundy guides became a mainstay, and Google bought it in 2011.
When these food guides, prizes and shows.Bocuse d'Or: Named for chef Paul Bocuse, this biennial contest in Lyon is called the "Olympics of cooking." Teams from dozens of countries compete.
When these food guides, prizes and shows.MasterChef (UK): The BBC show began in 1990 with Loyd Grossman as host. It was relaunched in 2005 with a more dramatic format that spread around the world.
When these food guides, prizes and shows.Food Network: Launched in the US in 1993, this channel turned chefs into celebrities. It was originally mostly instructional cooking shows.
When these food guides, prizes and shows.World's 50 Best Restaurants: Chefs, restaurateurs and critics vote for this annual list. It was launched by a British magazine, and has a well-known top spot.
When these food guides, prizes and shows.Yelp: Launched in San Francisco, Yelp made restaurant reviews crowd-sourced. Many restaurants feel its star ratings can make or break them.
When these food guides, prizes and shows.The Great British Bake Off: This baking contest began on BBC Two before moving to Channel 4 in 2017. It popularised the "soggy bottom" as a phrase.

Kings of Israel, then Judah, in biblical.Saul: Saul was the first king of a united Israel, said to be taller than everyone around him. He died in battle on Mount Gilboa.
Kings of Israel, then Judah, in biblical.David: The shepherd who beat Goliath became king and made Jerusalem his capital. The psalms are traditionally credited to him.
Kings of Israel, then Judah, in biblical.Solomon: Solomon built the First Temple in Jerusalem and was famed for his wisdom. His judgment between two women claiming one baby is legendary.
Kings of Israel, then Judah, in biblical.Rehoboam: Solomon's son Rehoboam answered a plea for lower taxes with a harsh reply. The kingdom then split into Israel in the north and Judah in the south.
Kings of Israel, then Judah, in biblical.Asa: Asa was one of Judah's reforming kings, who removed idols from the land. He ruled for more than 40 years.
Kings of Israel, then Judah, in biblical.Jehoshaphat: Jehoshaphat allied with Israel's King Ahab, and sent out officials to teach the law across Judah. He is remembered as a pious ruler.
Kings of Israel, then Judah, in biblical.Uzziah: Also called Azariah, Uzziah ruled about 52 years. He is said to have been struck with leprosy after he entered the Temple to burn incense.
Kings of Israel, then Judah, in biblical.Hezekiah: Hezekiah dug a tunnel to bring water into Jerusalem before the Assyrian siege. The Siloam Inscription found in it can still be seen.
Kings of Israel, then Judah, in biblical.Josiah: Josiah found a lost book of law in the Temple, which started a religious reform. He died fighting at Megiddo.
Kings of Israel, then Judah, in biblical.Zedekiah: The last king of Judah rebelled against Babylon. In 586 BC Jerusalem and the Temple were destroyed, and he was taken in chains.

When these cars were launched.Benz Patent-Motorwagen: Karl Benz patented this three-wheeler in 1886, and it's generally seen as the first true automobile. His wife Bertha made the first long-distance drive in one.
When these cars were launched.Ford Model T: Henry Ford's Model T put America on wheels, with over 15 million sold. Assembly-line production cut its price year after year.
When these cars were launched.Citroën 2CV: Designed to carry farmers and a basket of eggs across a ploughed field without breaking any, it was nicknamed the "umbrella on four wheels."
When these cars were launched.Mini: Alec Issigonis's tiny car put the engine sideways, to leave 80% of the floor for passengers and luggage. It became a 1960s icon.
When these cars were launched.Jaguar E-Type: Enzo Ferrari reportedly called it the most beautiful car ever made. Its long bonnet and low roof were inspired by racing cars.
When these cars were launched.Ford Mustang: It was launched at the 1964 World's Fair and created the "pony car" class. Ford sold over 22,000 on the first day.
When these cars were launched.Toyota Corolla: The Corolla is among the best-selling nameplates ever, with tens of millions sold. Its reliability built Toyota's global reputation.
When these cars were launched.DeLorean DMC-12: Its stainless-steel body and gull-wing doors starred in Back to the Future. The car was built in Northern Ireland, and the company soon collapsed.
When these cars were launched.Toyota Prius: The Prius was the first mass-produced hybrid car. It went on sale in Japan in 1997, before reaching the world.
When these cars were launched.Tesla Roadster: The electric sports car was built on a Lotus Elise chassis. One was famously launched into orbit around the Sun in 2018 aboard a rocket.

Alfred Hitchcock films by release.The 39 Steps: Adapted from John Buchan's novel, it set Hitchcock's template of an innocent man on the run.
Alfred Hitchcock films by release.Rebecca: His only film to win Best Picture; the title character is never seen on screen.
Alfred Hitchcock films by release.Notorious: Cary Grant and Ingrid Bergman chase Nazi spies over uranium hidden in wine bottles, with a famously long kiss.
Alfred Hitchcock films by release.Rear Window: Nearly all of it was filmed on one enormous set, a Greenwich Village courtyard built at Paramount.
Alfred Hitchcock films by release.Vertigo: The dolly-zoom effect, which stretches the background while the subject stays the same size, was devised for it.
Alfred Hitchcock films by release.North by Northwest: Features the crop-duster chase and a finale on Mount Rushmore.
Alfred Hitchcock films by release.Psycho: The shower scene took about a week to shoot, roughly 78 camera setups for a minute of film.
Alfred Hitchcock films by release.The Birds: It has no conventional score; its bird sounds were produced electronically with an instrument called the Trautonium.
Alfred Hitchcock films by release.Marnie: Tippi Hedren's second film with Hitchcock flopped at first, but critics have since reappraised it.
Alfred Hitchcock films by release.Frenzy: His late return to filming in London, a grim thriller about a necktie killer.

Queen Elizabeth II's life, in order.Born: She was born in Mayfair as third in line to the throne, and nobody expected her to become queen until her uncle abdicated in 1936.
Queen Elizabeth II's life, in order.Marries Prince Philip: Philip gave up his Greek and Danish titles to marry her; the Westminster Abbey wedding took place amid postwar rationing, and she saved clothing coupons for her gown.
Queen Elizabeth II's life, in order.Becomes queen: She was in Kenya, staying at the Treetops lodge, when her father died; she is said to have become queen while up a tree.
Queen Elizabeth II's life, in order.Coronation: Held in Westminster Abbey, it was the first coronation to be televised, and many Britons bought or borrowed a set just to watch it.
Queen Elizabeth II's life, in order.First TV Christmas message: Her Christmas broadcast began on radio in 1932 under her grandfather, but in 1957 viewers first saw the monarch deliver it live on television.
Queen Elizabeth II's life, in order.Silver Jubilee: Marking 25 years on the throne, it brought street parties across Britain, and the Sex Pistols released a rebellious single called God Save the Queen.
Queen Elizabeth II's life, in order.Golden Jubilee: It marked 50 years of her reign, in a year when she lost both her sister Princess Margaret and her mother, the Queen Mother.
Queen Elizabeth II's life, in order.Diamond Jubilee: About a thousand boats sailed down the Thames in the rain to mark 60 years; before her, only Queen Victoria had reigned that long.
Queen Elizabeth II's life, in order.Platinum Jubilee: She was the first British monarch to reach 70 years on the throne; the celebrations included a video of her having tea with Paddington Bear.
Queen Elizabeth II's life, in order.Dies: She died at Balmoral in Scotland aged 96, having reigned 70 years and 214 days, the longest of any British monarch.

Bill Murray films, by release year.Meatballs: His first starring role was as a camp counsellor, with much of it improvised, after he'd made his name on Saturday Night Live.
Bill Murray films, by release year.Caddyshack: Much of his role as the groundskeeper chasing a gopher was improvised, including the famous Dalai Lama speech.
Bill Murray films, by release year.Stripes: Directed by Ivan Reitman, this army comedy paired him with Harold Ramis, who co-wrote it.
Bill Murray films, by release year.Tootsie: His role as playwright roommate was uncredited, in a comedy that earned ten Oscar nominations.
Bill Murray films, by release year.Ghostbusters: The film's proton-pack gadgets made it one of the highest-grossing comedies of its decade.
Bill Murray films, by release year.Scrooged: A modern retelling of A Christmas Carol, in which he played a TV executive, Dickens's novella, published in 1843, has been adapted countless times.
Bill Murray films, by release year.Groundhog Day: His weatherman relives the same day over and over; Woodstock, Illinois stands in for Punxsutawney.
Bill Murray films, by release year.Rushmore: It began Murray's long run in Wes Anderson films.
Bill Murray films, by release year.Lost in Translation: It earned him an Oscar nomination as a fading star in Tokyo, and its whispered ending remains a famous mystery.
Bill Murray films, by release year.Zombieland: His cameo as himself, disguised as a zombie, turned into the film's surprise highlight.

Sandwich history.4th Earl of Sandwich born: John Montagu was First Lord of the Admiralty, and the town of Sandwich is in Kent.
Sandwich history.Sandwich named in print: The famous tale is that he ordered meat between bread to keep gambling; he may have been working.
Sandwich history.First PB&J recipe: A Boston cooking magazine printed the earliest recipe, and by World War II soldiers received it in rations.
Sandwich history.Reuben sandwich: Its origin is disputed between Omaha grocer Reuben Kulakofsky and New York's Arnold Reuben.
Sandwich history.Sliced bread sold: Otto Rohwedder invented the machine, and a bakery in Chillicothe, Missouri sold the first sliced loaf.
Sandwich history.Philly cheesesteak: Pat and Harry Olivieri sold hot dogs, and legend says a customer asked for steak, creating Pat's King of Steaks.
Sandwich history.Subway founded: Founded by 17-year-old Fred DeLuca with a $1,000 loan from Peter Buck, as Pete's Super Submarines.
Sandwich history.Big Mac introduced: Created by franchisee Jim Delligatti in Pittsburgh, and a jingle lists its ingredients.
